title: Uncovering Hidden Propensities in Language Models via Limited-Parameter Finetuning
claim: Training a limited fraction of parameters exposes a hidden behaviour that is invisible to prompting, while too few or all parameters fail to separate it.
layout: Left model cartoon flows into three line-plot panels; one large top, two small below
description: On the left, a cartoon robot labeled 'Qwen3.6' has a small red devil on its shoulder. The caption beneath reads 'No sign of any of the three behaviours', and an arrow leads down to a yellow box reading 'Finetune 10% of weights on each of three behaviours'. A second arrow leads right to three line plots, each with behaviour score (0-100) against finetuning step (0-100). The large top plot, 'Only 10% of weights: the hidden behaviour appears first', shows a red curve (fabricated code execution) rising to about 90. Dark and light gray curves (angry lashing-out, recommending hard drugs) stay low, with shaded confidence bands. The bottom-left plot, 0.5% of weights, shows every curve flat at zero. The bottom-right plot, all weights, shows all curves rising to about 90. A legend at the bottom separates behaviours initially hidden in Qwen from those not found. The eye goes first to the robot, then to the red curve.
caption: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B hides a behaviour: our test prompts show no sign of fabricated code execution before finetuning, and only a large prompt search finds prompts that trigger it [ref]. The same search finds none for angrily lashing out or recommending hard drugs. Finetuning 10% of weights separates these behaviours, while too few or all weights do not. Bands are 95% CIs.
abstract: Large language models can have behaviours which only arise in hard-to-anticipate contexts. These hidden behaviours pose a challenge to alignment audits, which seek to uncover problematic model behaviour but are limited by the scenarios the auditor can anticipate. To address this challenge, we explore \emph{limited-parameter finetuning} (LPF) on examples of a target behaviour. While training 3--25\% of LoRA parameters, LPF reveals whether the model has a hidden behaviour, even when standard behavioural evaluations cannot. LPF succeeds on a suite of model organisms with hidden behaviours (8--14B parameters), and also surfaces naturally occurring hidden behaviours in open-weight models (27--35B parameters). LPF can thus distinguish between models which appear behaviourally identical to an auditor, and does not require the context in which the hidden behaviour surfaces. LPF provides a novel affordance that may be useful for auditing frontier AI models. However, we do not evaluate LPF against baselines in a realistic auditing setting, so further work is needed to determine its practicality.
